# Sustainable Tourism Development Programme
## Destination Stewardship Framework — Recommendation for the Agency Board and Sponsoring Ministry

**Version 1.0 — complete. Prepared for board decision, and for prior circulation to district authorities, community and traditional-authority representatives, and the environment and antiquities agencies. Not yet for public or investor communication.**

---

### How we would ask you to use this

One note, then the substance.

This document does not propose a marketing campaign. It proposes the conditions under which a marketing campaign would be safe to run, and a sequence in which the campaign comes fourth rather than first. That ordering is the single most consequential thing in these pages, and if the board changes nothing else, we would ask it to consider changing that.

The site and locality material in §6 is offered as **working hypotheses, so that they can be corrected**. Where a district or community has its own data — or its own view of what it wants and does not want — that supersedes what we have written and the card is retired for that locality (§5.3). A card returned to us unamended will be read not as agreement but as a sign that the conversation has not yet happened, and we would come back for it.

Two courtesies before this travels further. First, that community and traditional-authority representatives see §§3, 9 and 12 and have time to respond in their own way before the ministerial pack is assembled — a programme about local authorship that arrives in a village fully formed has already contradicted itself, and people will notice that before they notice anything else. Second, that §12 (legal and consent gates) be walked through with the environment agency, the antiquities authority, the lands ministry and, where relevant, the national UNESCO commission before any part of this is described publicly. The likeliest single cause of avoidable damage is a well-intentioned announcement that reaches an investor before it reaches the people who live at the site.

---

## 1. Recommendation on a page

**Adopt a yield-and-retention strategy rather than a volume strategy: four place-and-community entitlements defined centrally as *floors*, with a formal alternative-form route where a floor cannot be met; product design, pricing, interpretation, pace and naming devolved entirely to districts and communities; a hypothecated visitor levy that makes conservation self-financing; four instrumented pilots of deliberately different design; and a published protocol binding the agency to the same discipline it asks of others.**

| | |
|---|---|
| Strategic objective | **Not more visitors. More value retained per unit of impact.** Target: visitor spend retained in-region rising from an assumed baseline of ~35% to 55%+ by Year 5, with ecological indicators stable or improving (§10) |
| Fixed nationally | **Four entitlements only** (§3) — ecological ceilings; local value capture; cultural authorship, including the right to withhold; an answered route for grievance. Each a floor, each with a named-approver alternative-form route (§3.6) |
| Devolved to districts and communities | Which visitors they seek, what is shown and what is not, pricing, interpretation, ritual, seasonality, tooling, pace, and the destination's own name. We would suggest the agency resist standardising even the name |
| Core instrument | **Hypothecated visitor levy** — bed-night and site-entry, ring-fenced by statute: 40% conservation, 35% community fund under local control, 15% infrastructure, 10% administration (§7.2) |
| Sequencing rule | **Plumbing before posters.** No international demand-generation spend in a locality until water, waste, sanitation and access capacity are verified against projected peak load (§14.1) |
| Year 1 shape | **Four pilots — one fragile ecosystem, one living-heritage settlement, one remote community-owned enterprise, one already-overloaded honeypot requiring de-load** — different in design, identical in instrumentation (§11) |
| Principal risk | Not visitor shortfall. **Elite capture and housing displacement** — value accruing to connected intermediaries, local and external, while residents absorb the costs (§13) |
| The agency's own obligation | **Published reversal protocol**: the agency may overturn a local decision, but must publish written reasons to the same audience that saw the decision, and reversal counts are reported quarterly beside destination metrics (§9.3) |
| Measurement | Retention, resident sentiment and ecological condition weighted 70%; arrival and revenue volume 30%. Volume alone never triggers a success declaration (§10) |
| Numeric failure test | International arrivals +20% or more while local retention is flat (±3pp) and resident sentiment declines = declared failure, marketing spend paused, capacity investment continues (§10.4) |
| Investment sought | **$6.8M Year 1, $14.5M Year 2** (illustrative, assumptions at §15.1), of which $2.1M is community enterprise finance and $1.3M is monitoring instrumentation — the two lines most often cut and most often fatal |
| Self-financing horizon | Levy revenue covers conservation and community fund operating cost from **Year 4**; the ask is bridging capital, not a permanent subsidy (§15.2) |
| Decisions requested | **Three** — §15.4 |
| Programme owner | Chief Executive, Tourism Agency, as sponsor; an independent Destination Stewardship Council with binding community seats constituted within 90 days of approval (§9) |

### 1.1 The core proposition, and how confident we are in it

Destinations rarely fail from too few visitors. They fail from visitors arriving faster than the capacity to absorb them and the arrangements to retain their money.

*(This is our considered assertion from practitioner experience and from comparative destination histories, not a finding derived from this region's own data — see the evidence key at §16. We flag it because the board is entitled to know which of our statements are evidenced and which are judgement.)*

The specific failure we are trying to avoid is well documented elsewhere and cheap to reproduce: a successful campaign, a three-year arrival surge concentrated on four photogenic sites, a housing market that prices out the people whose culture is the attraction, a leakage rate above 60%, and a resident population that has learned to resent the industry before the industry has learned to pay them. That outcome is worse than slow growth, because it consumes the local consent a second attempt would require. Consent, once spent, is not repurchasable at any budget.

---

## 2. Diagnosis before design

### 2.1 The framing we would gently ask the board to test

The programme is currently described as *attracting more international visitors*. The available evidence may instead describe a **value-retention and absorptive-capacity** problem wearing a marketing problem's clothing. Only one of those responds to promotion, and we would rather establish which we have before committing eight figures to the wrong one.

| Candidate constraint | What international demand-generation does to it |
|---|---|
| Genuine awareness deficit in target markets | Resolves it — this is the case where marketing is the right tool |
| Weak or absent local supply chain (food, guides, crafts, lodging) | **Amplifies harm** — demand met by imports and outside operators; leakage rises |
| Water, waste or sanitation at or near limit | **Amplifies harm** — irreversible ecological cost, and the first visible one |
| Access bottleneck (single road, single airport slot pattern) | Nothing — concentrates load rather than distributing it |
| Concentration on four sites while thirty are unvisited | Worsens — virality compounds concentration |
| Community consent not established at key sites | Worsens sharply — arrivals become an imposition, and resistance follows |
| Heritage fabric structurally fragile | **Amplifies harm** — footfall damage is cumulative and unfunded |
| Extreme seasonality producing precarious employment | Nothing — needs product design for shoulder seasons, not more shoulder-season adverts |

### 2.2 The diagnostic we propose

Twelve weeks, no design freeze and no campaign commitment until it reports:

- **Carrying-capacity assessment** at the twelve highest-pressure sites — ecological, physical, infrastructural and social thresholds, each expressed as a number with a stated confidence interval;
- **Leakage and value-chain study** — where each unit of visitor spend goes, by category, ownership and residence of owner;
- **Resident sentiment baseline** in fourteen localities, disaggregated by age, gender and livelihood, before any promotion begins, so that later movement is interpretable;
- **Consent and tenure mapping** — who holds what rights over which sites, formally and customarily, and where those two registers disagree;
- **Heritage condition survey** — structural and fabric baseline, with footfall sensitivity noted;
- **Water and waste stress test** against three projected peak-load scenarios.

Cost **$620K**. If the study finds that leakage exceeds 55% or that any of the four flagship sites is within 15% of an ecological threshold, the Year 2 promotion envelope should be redirected to supply-side development and capacity works, and the pilot scope revised before commitment. This is the cheapest consequential decision in the programme.

### 2.3 The uncomfortable question, answered rather than deferred

Will the agency be bound by the same entitlements it asks of others? If a district discovers that the agency can overturn a locally-taken decision without giving reasons — or can license a resort inside a locality that declined one — the framework becomes rhetoric and everything downstream of it is wasted. §9.3 answers this with a specific, testable, reportable mechanism, and we would ask the board to adopt or amend it rather than to note it.

---

## 3. What is fixed everywhere: four entitlements, stated as floors

Framed as what a place and its residents are entitled to, rather than as how an operator must behave, so that very different arrangements can honour them.

### 3.1 Entitlement I — ecological ceilings are numbers, and they bind
**Floor:** every designated site has a published maximum daily and peak-hour visitor number, derived from measured thresholds, reviewed annually, and enforceable against every operator including state-owned ones. Where measurement is incomplete, an interim ceiling is set at the conservative end and revised upward only on evidence — never downward under commercial pressure alone.

*The ceiling is the ceiling. A ceiling that rises whenever it is reached is not a ceiling; it is a queue-management aspiration.*

### 3.2 Entitlement II — local value capture has a floor, not an aspiration
**Floor:** in any licensed tourism operation above a defined size, (a) a minimum share of employment at supervisory level and above is held by residents of the district, on a stated glide path rather than immediately; (b) a minimum share of food, craft and service procurement is sourced within the region, verified by audit rather than by declaration; (c) concession revenue from public land and heritage sites returns a defined percentage to the locality under local control.

We would suggest glide paths with dated milestones rather than day-one quotas. A quota that cannot be met produces either non-compliance or imported "residents"; a glide path with a funded training pipeline produces the outcome the quota was reaching for.

### 3.3 Entitlement III — cultural authorship, including the right to withhold
**Floor:** the community associated with a cultural practice, site or artefact decides what is presented to visitors, in what form, at what price, and whether it is presented at all. This includes an unconditional **right to withhold** — some things are not products, and a framework that cannot say so will eventually be asked to sell them.

Practically: no ceremony scheduled for visitor convenience without the custodians' initiative; no photography where custodians have declined it; interpretation texts approved by the community before publication, in their language first; sacred and restricted sites may be closed permanently and that closure is not appealable on commercial grounds.

### 3.4 Entitlement IV — there is a route for grievance, and it is answered
**Floor:** every resident of a tourism locality has at least one accessible channel through which they can object to a tourism development, operator behaviour or agency decision **and receive a dated, substantive response**. Form is local: a village assembly, a district ombudsman, a written pre-read, a monthly market-day surgery, an SMS line. The *answered* part is the floor; the form is entirely local.

**Firewall, mandatory:** this channel is expressly **not** a corruption or safeguarding reporting channel. Objection to a development is not a protected disclosure. The two must be separately named, separately routed and separately governed, or we create legal exposure on one side and chill genuine reporting on the other (§12.4).

### 3.5 Everything else is local property
Product design, pricing, interpretation, ceremony, sequencing, symbolism, tooling, partner selection, target segments, pace, and the destination's own name.

### 3.6 The alternative-form process (in place of exemption)

We deliberately avoid the word *exemption*, and avoid asking any district to refuse. A locality that cannot meet a floor is asked instead to **propose the nearest form it can honour**, and to state what it would take to close the remainder.

| Element | Provision |
|---|---|
| Trigger | Legal impossibility, tenure conflict, or structural impossibility (not difficulty, not commercial inconvenience) |
| Form | Two pages: which floor, why, the alternative mechanism proposed, and the condition under which the floor becomes reachable |
| Approver | Chief Executive of the agency, countersigned by the district authority and the relevant sectoral regulator |
| Duration | **24 months maximum**, renewable once with fresh reasoning |
| Visibility | Entered in a publicly accessible register, reviewed quarterly by the Stewardship Council |
| Presumption | An alternative form is accepted unless materially weaker than the floor. We expect three to six across the network in Year 1 and would be suspicious of zero |
| Never available | Entitlement I ecological ceilings, and the right to withhold under III. These two do not admit alternative forms |

---

## 4. The adaptation logic

### 4.1 Four variables, rather than a general destination model

We would ask each locality to place itself on four axes only, because these four determine whether a given tourism form functions or backfires.

| Axis | The question | What it changes |
|---|---|---|
| **Fragility** | How quickly does damage become irreversible? | Whether the instrument is a cap and permit, or a price signal |
| **Livedness** | Is the site inhabited, worked and used, or is it a monument? | Whether residents can be zoned around, or must be the authors |
| **Existing load** | Is the locality below capacity, near it, or past it? | Whether the task is attraction or de-load — opposite disciplines |
| **Local enterprise depth** | Can local businesses supply what visitors need today? | Whether promotion creates income or creates imports |

### 4.2 The working rule

> Fragility and high existing load do not mean tourism is unwelcome. They mean the growth has to be **in value rather than in volume** — fewer visitors, longer stays, higher spend, deeper local sourcing, dispersed across geography and season.

The functioning equivalent of a marketing campaign, in a locality already at load, is a permit system with dynamic pricing, a second and third route that draws pressure outward, and a shoulder-season product that gives residents twelve months of work instead of four. Our practitioner judgement is that a single well-designed dispersal route moves more economic benefit than a quarter of promotional spend — offered as judgement, not as measured finding (§16), and testable inside the pilots.

### 4.3 Local leadership: a default with a visible opt-out

**Default:** locality-level programme leadership sits with people already running functioning local enterprises or already holding custodial responsibility — selected on observed practice rather than on office held.

A district wishing to depart from this default does so through a one-page note countersigned by the district authority and the programme director, logged in the same register as §3.6. Departures are expected and unremarkable; what matters is that they are visible.

Where the practitioner lead sits outside formal authority, the workable form is almost always a **pair** — the office-holder as visible patron providing cover, the practitioner as the working engine. A practitioner without a patron will in several districts be read, reasonably, as the agency not taking the district seriously.

---

## 5. Using the locality cards well

### 5.1 What they are
Starting hypotheses about context, to be returned marked up within 60 days. They describe patterns we have observed in destinations, not judgements about people.

### 5.2 What each card contains
Working hypothesis on the four axes · where the binding constraint likely sits · what to build · what to decline · failure mode · **leading indicator observable by day 90** · legal, tenure or consent watch item.

### 5.3 The supersession rule
**Where locality-level diagnostic data exists, it supersedes the card, and the card is retired for that locality.** Within-district variance routinely exceeds between-district variance; a single village's history with an earlier development frequently dominates every regional generalisation we could offer.

---

## 6. Locality typology cards

### Card A — Fragile ecosystem, low current load
| | |
|---|---|
| Hypothesis | High fragility; uninhabited or lightly inhabited; well below load; thin local enterprise base |
| Binding constraint | Absence of a ceiling *before* discovery. Once a site is popular, imposing a cap is a political act; before, it is administration |
| Build | Permit system with dynamic pricing and advance ballot; mandatory accredited local guiding; hardened trails and viewing infrastructure ahead of demand; a research and monitoring station co-located with the visitor function |
| Decline | Road upgrades that reduce journey time below the friction the ecosystem depends on; any accommodation inside the boundary; cruise or coach access without a berth/slot cap |
| Failure mode | Single viral image, arrivals treble in eighteen months, ceiling set retrospectively

# Global Employee Empowerment & Adaptive Culture Initiative
## Guidance on Regional Leadership Adaptation — Recommendation for Sponsor Group

**Version 2.0 — complete. Prepared for sponsor group decision, and for prior circulation to the fourteen regional people leads. Not yet for employee communication.**

---

### How we would ask you to use this

One note only, and then the substance.

This version differs from v1.0 in three ways that the reviewers were right to insist on. It now asks for specific decisions, with money and a date attached (§12). It answers the questions the first draft deferred — most importantly what the centre itself is bound by (§9). And the regional material has been re-cut so that no colleague opens it and finds their country described inside someone else's card.

The regional cards in §6 remain what they were: **working hypotheses, offered so that they can be corrected**. Where a region has its own diagnostic data, that data replaces the card and the card is retired for that unit (§5.4). A card returned to us unamended will be read not as agreement but as a sign that the conversation has not yet taken place, and we would come back for it.

Two courtesies we would ask the sponsor group to extend before this travels further. First, that the fourteen regional people leads and the four regional MDs see §§3, 4 and 9 and have time to respond in their own way before the board pack is assembled — a programme about devolved authority that arrives in a region fully formed has already contradicted itself, and colleagues will notice that before they notice anything else. Second, that §10 (consultation and legal gates) be walked through with Group Legal, the European Works Council secretariat and Group Reward before any part of this is described to employees anywhere. The likeliest single cause of avoidable damage is a well-intentioned announcement that reaches a works council after it reaches a newspaper, or reaches an employee before it reaches their own supervisor.

---

## 1. Recommendation on a page

**Adopt a thin global core and a wide local expression: four employee entitlements defined centrally as *floors*, with a formal alternative-form process where a floor cannot lawfully or structurally be met; delivery method, language, sequencing and naming devolved entirely to regions; four instrumented pilots in Year 1 with a common measurement spine but deliberately different local design; and a published protocol binding the centre to the same discipline it asks of others.**

| | |
|---|---|
| Global mandate | **Four entitlements only** (§3) — decision rights at the lowest competent level; an answered route for dissent; tolerance of good-faith error; employee-initiated internal movement. Each stated as a floor, each with a named-approver alternative-form route (§3.6) |
| Devolved to regions | Language, ritual, sequencing, symbolism, manager incentives, pace, communication channels, and the programme's name. We would suggest the centre resist standardising even the name |
| Year 1 shape | **Four pilots — one high-authority-distance, one low, one deskless-majority, one recently-acquired entity** — different in design, identical in instrumentation (§7) |
| Principal risk | Middle-manager status and grade loss, not employee resistance (§8) |
| The centre's own obligation | **Published reversal protocol**: the centre may reverse a devolved decision, but must give written reasons to the same audience that saw the decision, and reversal counts are reported quarterly beside regional metrics (§9) |
| Measurement | Within-region trend on four behavioural proxies weighted 70%, survey items 30%; acquiescence correction applied before any cross-region view is shown (§8.3) |
| Numeric failure test | Empowerment survey index +5 points or more while decision latency on the instrumented decision class improves <10% and internal-move rate is flat = declared failure, programme paused, no further capital (§8.5) |
| Investment sought | **$14.2M Year 1, $10.6M Year 2** (illustrative, assumptions in §12.1), of which $6.9M is manager time relief — the line most often omitted and most often fatal |
| Funding split | Central P&L funds diagnostic, instrumentation, platform, central team and pilot facilitation; regions fund manager time with a **60% central offset in Y1, 30% in Y2, nil thereafter** (§12.3) |
| Decisions requested | **Three** — §12.5, sought at the sponsor group meeting on **18 March** |
| Programme owner | Group Chief People Officer, sponsor; named programme director recruited internally within 30 days of approval |

### 1.1 The core proposition, and how confident we are in it

Empowerment mechanisms do not transfer between contexts; the conditions that make them work can be built in each. *(This is our considered assertion from practitioner experience, not a finding — see the evidence key at §14. We flag it because the sponsor group is entitled to know which of our statements are evidenced and which are judgement.)*

The specific failure we are trying to avoid is well documented in our own past programmes: exported behavioural vocabulary — "speak up", "own it", "disagree and commit" — produces regions that become fluent at the annual survey and unchanged on Tuesday morning. That outcome is worse than no initiative, because it consumes the credibility a second attempt would require.

---

## 2. Diagnosis before we design

### 2.1 The framing we would gently ask the sponsor group to test

The initiative is currently described as culture change. The evidence available to us may instead describe a **decision-rights and information-flow** problem wearing culture-change clothing. Only one of those two responds to leadership behaviour work, and we would rather establish which we have before committing eight figures to the wrong one.

| Candidate driver | What leadership/empowerment training does to it |
|---|---|
| Decision rights formally held too high | Nothing — requires delegation-of-authority redesign |
| Rights delegated on paper, retracted in practice | Nothing until retraction is made visible and costly (§9) |
| Information does not reach the level holding authority | **Amplifies harm** — confident decisions on poor data |
| Managers lack coaching capability | Improves, *if* paired with funded time relief (§8.4) |
| Reward and grading pay for control, not for developing others | Nothing — the incentive wins every time (§8.2) |
| Employees have voice but no evidence it is ever acted on | Worsens — a further unanswered invitation deepens cynicism |
| Working-language barrier suppresses contribution | Nothing — needs channel design, not confidence-building (§11.1) |

### 2.2 The diagnostic we propose

Five weeks, no design freeze until it reports: 60 structured conversations across four organisational levels in eight countries (including two deskless-majority sites); an audit of the documented delegation-of-authority matrix against actual practice in twelve units; and a language-barrier check in the four sites where the working language is not the local one. Cost **$310K**.

If it finds that decision rights are formally too high, the largest part of the Year 2 training envelope should be redirected to delegation architecture and the pilot scope revised before commitment. This is the cheapest consequential decision in the programme.

### 2.3 The uncomfortable question, now answered rather than deferred

Will headquarters be bound by the same four entitlements? If regional colleagues discover that the centre reserves the right to overturn devolved decisions without giving reasons, the initiative becomes rhetoric and everything downstream of it is wasted. v1.0 left this open. **§9 now answers it with a specific, testable, reportable mechanism**, and we would ask the sponsor group to adopt or amend it rather than to note it.

---

## 3. What is fixed everywhere: four entitlements, stated as floors

Framed as what an employee is entitled to, not as how a manager must behave, so that very different conduct can honour them.

### 3.1 Entitlement I — decision rights sit at the lowest competent level
**Floor:** every employee can name the classes of decision they own and point to a recent instance of exercising one without seeking permission. *Competent* is doing real work in that sentence; this is not an argument for uniform flat structures.

### 3.2 Entitlement II — there is a route for dissent, and it is answered
**Floor:** every employee has at least one available channel through which they can contradict a superior's view **and receive a response**. The channel may be a written pre-read, a skip-level, a facilitated small group, a mentor, a shift huddle, or an anonymous board. It need never be a raised hand in a large meeting. The answered part is the floor; the form is entirely local.

**Firewall, mandatory:** this channel is expressly **not** a statutory reporting channel. Disagreement about a business decision is not a protected disclosure. The two must be separately named, separately routed and separately governed, or we create legal exposure on one side and chill genuine reporting on the other (§10.3).

### 3.3 Entitlement III — good-faith error is absorbed, not attributed
**Floor:** within each unit, at least one specific, visible instance per quarter in which a good-faith mistake was absorbed rather than attributed, and the team can name it. Demonstrated, never announced. In several regions this must be framed collectively rather than individually to be usable at all (§6).

### 3.4 Entitlement IV — employees can initiate their own movement
**Floor (revised from v1.0):** an employee may apply for an internal role, project or rotation **without the incumbent manager holding a veto and without the manager being informed in advance of the application**.

v1.0 stated this as an absolute and was wrong to. In parts of the Gulf, mobility between entities is constrained by employer-tied work permits and is a legal matter, not a cultural one. In Japan, Korea and Taiwan, seniority-anchored career and reward structures make unrestricted lateral self-nomination structurally disruptive in ways that a global mandate cannot responsibly overrule from a distance. The floor above is the most we can hold everywhere; where even that cannot be met, §3.6 applies.

### 3.5 Everything else is regional property
Language, ceremony, sequencing, symbolism, tooling, incentives, cadence, and the programme's own name.

### 3.6 The alternative-form process (in place of exemption)

We deliberately avoid the word *exemption*, and avoid asking any region to refuse. A region that cannot meet a floor is asked instead to **propose the nearest form it can honour**, and to say what it would take to close the remainder.

| Element | Provision |
|---|---|
| Trigger | Legal impossibility, collective-agreement conflict, or structural impossibility (not difficulty, not discomfort) |
| Form | Two pages: which floor, why, the alternative mechanism proposed, and the condition under which the floor becomes reachable |
| Approver | **Group Chief People Officer**, countersigned by the Regional MD and by Group Legal |
| Duration | **12 months maximum**, renewable once with fresh reasoning |
| Visibility | Entered in an internally published register, reviewed quarterly by the sponsor group |
| Presumption | An alternative form is accepted unless it is materially weaker than the floor. We expect four to eight across the network in Year 1 and would be suspicious of zero |

---

## 4. The adaptation logic

### 4.1 Four variables, rather than a general culture model

We would ask each region to place itself on four axes only, because these four determine whether a given mechanism functions or backfires.

| Axis | The question | What it changes |
|---|---|---|
| **Authority basis** | Does a manager's authority derive from role or from demonstrated expertise? | Whether devolution reads as trust or as abandonment |
| **Directness of disagreement** | Can dissent be public without cost to either party? | The design of the dissent channel (Entitlement II) |
| **Attribution of error** | Does a mistake attach to a person, a team, or a system? | Whether error tolerance can be individual or must be collective (III) |
| **Ambiguity tolerance** | Is an open brief experienced as freedom, or as information withheld? | How much structure must accompany autonomy |

### 4.2 The working rule

> High authority distance and low disagreement-directness do not mean empowerment is unwelcome. They mean it must be **granted rather than seized** — granted visibly, specifically, bounded, and by someone whose authority the team already accepts.

In such contexts an open invitation ("bring me your ideas") is not empowerment; it is a test most colleagues will decline to sit. The functioning equivalent is a named, bounded, publicly conferred mandate: *"Priya decides this class of exception up to this threshold. She does not need to ask me. If you disagree with her, take it to her."* Our practitioner judgement is that this single act moves more behaviour than a quarter of workshops — offered as judgement, not as measured finding (§14), and testable inside the pilots via the decision-latency proxy.

### 4.3 Sponsorship: a default with a visible opt-out

**Default:** regional sponsors are selected on observed practice — leaders whose own teams already exhibit the four entitlements — rather than on rank.

We acknowledged in v1.0 that this backfires in several regions, then handed the choice back, which was no recommendation at all. The corrected position: the default stands, and a region wishing to depart from it does so through a **one-page note countersigned by the Regional MD and the programme director**, logged in the same register as §3.6. Departures are expected and unremarkable; what matters is that they are visible.

Where the practitioner sponsor sits two or three levels below the Regional MD, the workable form is almost always a **pair** — the senior figure as visible patron providing cover and air, the practitioner as the working engine. A junior sponsor without a senior patron will in several regions be read, reasonably, as the centre not taking the region seriously.

---

## 5. Using the regional cards well

### 5.1 What they are
Starting hypotheses about context, to be returned marked up within 45 days. They describe patterns we have observed in workplaces, not peoples.

### 5.2 What each card contains
Working hypothesis on the four axes · where the gap likely sits · behaviour to add · behaviour to drop · failure mode · **leading indicator observable by day 60** · legal or structural watch item.

### 5.3 The 60-day indicator, and why it is on every card
The failure modes that matter most — courteous non-adoption, affirmative response with no movement — are precisely the ones you cannot detect by asking. Each card therefore names an observable proxy visible within 60 days.

### 5.4 The supersession rule
**Where unit-level diagnostic data exists, it supersedes the card, and the card is retired for that unit.** Within-country variance in work values routinely exceeds between-country variance; function, site history and acquisition lineage frequently dominate nationality. This applies to every card, not only where we have noted it.

### 5.5 Scope note
Cards cover the fourteen clusters where we have wholly-owned or majority-controlled operations. Russia and Belarus are **out of scope** for this programme pending the Group's standing position on those entities; the programme director should not open a workstream there without a written instruction from the sponsor group.

---

## 6. Regional cards

### Card A — Anglosphere (US, Canada, UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand)

| | |
|---|---|

### 4.1 Four variables, rather than a general destination model

Destinations rarely fail from too few visitors. They fail from visitors arriving faster than the capacity to absorb them and the arrangements to retain their money.

The specific failure we are trying to avoid is well documented elsewhere and cheap to reproduce: a successful campaign, a three-year arrival surge concentrated on four photogenic sites, a housing market that prices out the people whose culture is the attraction, a leakage rate above 60%, and a resident population that has learned to resent the industry before the industry has learned to pay them. ## 2. Diagnosis before design

### 2.1 The framing we would gently ask the board to test

The programme is currently described as *attracting more international visitors*. The available evidence may instead describe a **value-retention and absorptive-capacity** problem wearing a marketing problem's clothing. Only one of those responds to promotion, and we would rather establish which we have before committing eight figures to the wrong one.

| Candidate constraint | What international demand-generation does to it |
|---|---|
| Genuine awareness deficit in target markets | Resolves it — this is the case where marketing is the right tool |
| Weak or absent local supply chain (food, guides, crafts, lodging) | **Amplifies harm** — demand met by imports and outside operators; leakage rises |
| Water, waste or sanitation at or near limit | **Amplifies harm** — irreversible ecological cost, and the first visible one |
| Access bottleneck (single road, single airport slot pattern) | Nothing — concentrates load rather than distributing it |
| Concentration on four sites while thirty are unvisited | Worsens — virality compounds concentration |
| Community consent not established at key sites | Worsens sharply — arrivals become an imposition, and resistance follows |
| Heritage fabric structurally fragile | **Amplifies harm** — footfall damage is cumulative and unfunded |
| Extreme seasonality producing precarious employment | Nothing — needs product design for shoulder seasons, not more shoulder-season adverts |

### 2.2 The diagnostic we propose

Twelve weeks, no design freeze and no campaign commitment until it reports:

- **Carrying-capacity assessment** at the twelve highest-pressure sites — ecological, physical, infrastructural and social thresholds, each expressed as a number with a stated confidence interval;
- **Leakage and value-chain study** — where each unit of visitor spend goes, by category, ownership and residence of owner;
- **Resident sentiment baseline** in fourteen localities, disaggregated by age, gender and livelihood, before any promotion begins, so that later movement is interpretable;
- **Consent and tenure mapping** — who holds what rights over which sites, formally and customarily, and where those two registers disagree;
- **Heritage condition survey** — structural and fabric baseline, with footfall sensitivity noted;
- **Water and waste stress test** against three projected peak-load scenarios.

Cost **$620K**. If the study finds that leakage exceeds 55% or that any of the four flagship sites is within 15% of an ecological threshold, the Year 2 promotion envelope should be redirected to supply-side development and capacity works, and the pilot scope revised before commitment. This is the cheapest consequential decision in the programme.

### 2.3 The uncomfortable question, answered rather than deferred

Will the agency be bound by the same entitlements it asks of others? If a district discovers that the agency can overturn a locally-taken decision without giving reasons — or can license a resort inside a locality that declined one — the framework becomes rhetoric and everything downstream of it is wasted. §9.3 answers this with a specific, testable, reportable mechanism, and we would ask the board to adopt or amend it rather than to note it.

## 3. What is fixed everywhere: four entitlements, stated as floors

Framed as what a place and its residents are entitled to, rather than as how an operator must behave, so that very different arrangements can honour them.

### 3.1 Entitlement I — ecological ceilings are numbers, and they bind
**Floor:** every designated site has a published maximum daily and peak-hour visitor number, derived from measured thresholds, reviewed annually, and enforceable against every operator including state-owned ones. Where measurement is incomplete, an interim ceiling is set at the conservative end and revised upward only on evidence — never downward under commercial pressure alone.

*The ceiling is the ceiling. A ceiling that rises whenever it is reached is not a ceiling; it is a queue-management aspiration.*

### 3.2 Entitlement II — local value capture has a floor, not an aspiration
**Floor:** in any licensed tourism operation above a defined size, (a) a minimum share of employment at supervisory level and above is held by residents of the district, on a stated glide path rather than immediately; (b) a minimum share of food, craft and service procurement is sourced within the region, verified by audit rather than by declaration; (c) concession revenue from public land and heritage sites returns a defined percentage to the locality under local control.

We would suggest glide paths with dated milestones rather than day-one quotas. A quota that cannot be met produces either non-compliance or imported "residents"; a glide path with a funded training pipeline produces the outcome the quota was reaching for.

### 3.3 Entitlement III — cultural authorship, including the right to withhold
**Floor:** the community associated with a cultural practice, site or artefact decides what is presented to visitors, in what form, at what price, and whether it is presented at all. This includes an unconditional **right to withhold** — some things are not products, and a framework that cannot say so will eventually be asked to sell them.

Practically: no ceremony scheduled for visitor convenience without the custodians' initiative; no photography where custodians have declined it; interpretation texts approved by the community before publication, in their language first; sacred and restricted sites may be closed permanently and that closure is not appealable on commercial grounds.

### 3.4 Entitlement IV — there is a route for grievance, and it is answered
**Floor:** every resident of a tourism locality has at least one accessible channel through which they can object to a tourism development, operator behaviour or agency decision **and receive a dated, substantive response**. Form is local: a village assembly, a district ombudsman, a written pre-read, a monthly market-day surgery, an SMS line. The *answered* part is the floor; the form is entirely local.

**Firewall, mandatory:** this channel is expressly **not** a corruption or safeguarding reporting channel. Objection to a development is not a protected disclosure. The two must be separately named, separately routed and separately governed, or we create legal exposure on one side and chill genuine reporting on the other (§12.4).

### 3.5 Everything else is local property
Product design, pricing, interpretation, ceremony, sequencing, symbolism, tooling, partner selection, target segments, pace, and the destination's own name.

### 3.6 The alternative-form process (in place of exemption)

We deliberately avoid the word *exemption*, and avoid asking any district to refuse. A locality that cannot meet a floor is asked instead to **propose the nearest form it can honour**, and to state what it would take to close the remainder.

|---|---|
| Trigger | Legal impossibility, tenure conflict, or structural impossibility (not difficulty, not commercial inconvenience) |
| Form | Two pages: which floor, why, the alternative mechanism proposed, and the condition under which the floor becomes reachable |
| Approver | Chief Executive of the agency, countersigned by the district authority and the relevant sectoral regulator |
| Duration | **24 months maximum**, renewable once with fresh reasoning |
| Visibility | Entered in a publicly accessible register, reviewed quarterly by the Stewardship Council |
| Presumption | An alternative form is accepted unless materially weaker than the floor. We expect three to six across the network in Year 1 and would be suspicious of zero |
| Never available | Entitlement I ecological ceilings, and the right to withhold under III. These two do not admit alternative forms |

## 4. The adaptation logic

### 4.1 Four variables, rather than a general destination model

We would ask each locality to place itself on four axes only, because these four determine whether a given tourism form functions or backfires.

| Axis | The question | What it changes |
|---|---|---|
| **Fragility** | How quickly does damage become irreversible? | Whether the instrument is a cap and permit, or a price signal |
| **Livedness** | Is the site inhabited, worked and used, or is it a monument? | Whether residents can be zoned around, or must be the authors |
| **Existing load** | Is the locality below capacity, near it, or past it? | Whether the task is attraction or de-load — opposite disciplines |
| **Local enterprise depth** | Can local businesses supply what visitors need today? | Whether promotion creates income or creates imports |

### 4.2 The working rule

> Fragility and high existing load do not mean tourism is unwelcome. They mean the growth has to be **in value rather than in volume** — fewer visitors, longer stays, higher spend, deeper local sourcing, dispersed across geography and season.

The functioning equivalent of a marketing campaign, in a locality already at load, is a permit system with dynamic pricing, a second and third route that draws pressure outward, and a shoulder-season product that gives residents twelve months of work instead of four. Our practitioner judgement is that a single well-designed dispersal route moves more economic benefit than a quarter of promotional spend — offered as judgement, not as measured finding (§16), and testable inside the pilots.

### 4.3 Local leadership: a default with a visible opt-out

**Default:** locality-level programme leadership sits with people already running functioning local enterprises or already holding custodial responsibility — selected on observed practice rather than on office held.

A district wishing to depart from this default does so through a one-page note countersigned by the district authority and the programme director, logged in the same register as §3.6. Departures are expected and unremarkable; what matters is that they are visible.

Where the practitioner lead sits outside formal authority, the workable form is almost always a **pair** — the office-holder as visible patron providing cover, the practitioner as the working engine. A practitioner without a patron will in several districts be read, reasonably, as the agency not taking the district seriously.

**2.1 A self-created conflict of interest the document does not notice.** The levy allocates **10% to administration** — i.e. the agency's own budget scales with visitor volume — while the same agency chairs the body that reviews ecological ceilings and holds §3.6 approval authority. §3.1 permits ceilings to be "revised upward only on evidence," but names no independent evidence assessor. In most jurisdictions a tourism agency has none of these powers — they sit with environment, antiquities, lands, labour and finance ministries, and hypothecation is routinely resisted by treasuries. The document lists those bodies as *consultees* (§12) rather than as co-holders of the instruments. **The Ministry of Finance is not mentioned at all.** Required: a legal instruments annex mapping each entitlement to the statute, regulation, licence condition or intergovernmental agreement that would carry it, with a legislative timeline. The total ask is $6.8M + $14.5M. Utility and access capital works across twelve high-pressure sites will exceed that by an order of magnitude in almost any real region. Either the programme funds the works (budget is wrong by 10×) or it does not (in which case the rule is a veto the programme cannot lift, and the whole plan stalls at Year 2). This must be resolved explicitly: state the capacity-works estimate, name the funding source — municipal capital, sovereign borrowing, IFI/donor concessional finance, PPP — and treat it as a precondition rather than an assumption.

**2.4 The headline target contradicts the diagnostic discipline.** §1 sets retention 35% → 55% off an **assumed** baseline; §2.2 says no design freeze until the leakage study reports. Publishing a target before measuring the baseline is precisely the error the document criticises elsewhere. Present it as an illustrative ambition to be re-set at diagnostic close.

**2.5 The failure test may be unfalsifiable.** "Retention flat (±3pp)" implies value-chain measurement precise to three percentage points. Leakage studies rarely achieve that; sampling error alone will exceed it. State the measurement method, sample and confidence interval, or widen the band. Also state *when* the test first runs — if Year 1 has no promotion, a test keyed to "+20% arrivals" cannot fire until Year 3.

**2.6 The 70/30 weighting is asserted, not constructed.** Retention, resident sentiment and ecological condition are three dissimilar quantities in different units. Needed: a recognition-and-dispute procedure specifying who is treated as the decision-holder, how disagreement is adjudicated, and what happens while it is unresolved (default: nothing proceeds).

**2.8 Consent language stops short.** For a programme touching traditional authorities, sacred sites and possibly indigenous peoples, **Free, Prior and Informed Consent is never named**, nor are UNDRIP/ILO 169 or national consent law. Naming the standard costs nothing and materially strengthens both legitimacy and defensibility with UNESCO, IFIs and international operators.

**3.4 Incumbents and political economy.** The plan reads as though the industry does not yet exist. ### How we would ask you to use this

One note, then the substance.

This document does not propose a marketing campaign. It proposes the conditions under which a marketing campaign would be safe to run, and a sequence in which the campaign comes fourth rather than first. That ordering is the single most consequential thing in these pages, and if the board changes nothing else, we would ask it to consider changing that.

The site and locality material in §6 is offered as **working hypotheses, so that they can be corrected**. Where a district or community has its own data — or its own view of what it wants and does not want — that supersedes what we have written and the card is retired for that locality (§5.3). First, that community and traditional-authority representatives see §§3, 9 and 12 and have time to respond in their own way before the ministerial pack is assembled — a programme about local authorship that arrives in a village fully formed has already contradicted itself, and people will notice that before they notice anything else. ---

## 1. Recommendation on a page

**Adopt a yield-and-retention strategy rather than a volume strategy: four place-and-community entitlements defined centrally as *floors*, with a formal alternative-form route where a floor cannot be met; product design, pricing, interpretation, pace and naming devolved entirely to districts and communities; a hypothecated visitor levy that makes conservation self-financing; four instrumented pilots of deliberately different design; and a published protocol binding the agency to the same discipline it asks of others.**

| Sequencing rule | **Plumbing before posters.** No international demand-generation spend in a locality until water, waste, sanitation and access capacity are verified against projected peak load (§14.1) |
| Year 1 shape | **Four pilots — one fragile ecosystem, one living-heritage settlement, one remote community-owned enterprise, one already-overloaded honeypot requiring de-load** — different in design, identical in instrumentation (§11) |

### 1.1 The core proposition, and how confident we are in it

Destinations rarely fail from too few visitors. They fail from visitors arriving faster than the capacity to absorb them and the arrangements to retain their money.

*(This is our considered assertion from practitioner experience and from comparative destination histories, not a finding derived from this region's own data — see the evidence key at §16. We flag it because the board is entitled to know which of our statements are evidenced and which are judgement.)*

The specific failure we are trying to avoid is well documented elsewhere and cheap to reproduce: a successful campaign, a three-year arrival surge concentrated on four photogenic sites, a housing market that prices out the people whose culture is the attraction, a leakage rate above 60%, and a resident population that has learned to resent the industry before the industry has learned to pay them. That outcome is worse than slow growth, because it consumes the local consent a second attempt would require. Consent, once spent, is not repurchasable at any budget.

---

## 2. Diagnosis before design

### 2.1 The framing we would gently ask the board to test

The programme is currently described as *attracting more international visitors*. The available evidence may instead describe a **value-retention and absorptive-capacity** problem wearing a marketing problem's clothing. Only one of those responds to promotion, and we would rather establish which we have before committing eight figures to the wrong one.

| Candidate constraint | What international demand-generation does to it |
|---|---|
| Genuine awareness deficit in target markets | Resolves it — this is the case where marketing is the right tool |
| Weak or absent local supply chain (food, guides, crafts, lodging) | **Amplifies harm** — demand met by imports and outside operators; leakage rises |
| Water, waste or sanitation at or near limit | **Amplifies harm** — irreversible ecological cost, and the first visible one |
| Access bottleneck (single road, single airport slot pattern) | Nothing — concentrates load rather than distributing it |
| Concentration on four sites while thirty are unvisited | Worsens — virality compounds concentration |
| Community consent not established at key sites | Worsens sharply — arrivals become an imposition, and resistance follows |
| Heritage fabric structurally fragile | **Amplifies harm** — footfall damage is cumulative and unfunded |
| Extreme seasonality producing precarious employment | Nothing — needs product design for shoulder seasons, not more shoulder-season adverts |

### 2.2 The diagnostic we propose

Twelve weeks, no design freeze and no campaign commitment until it reports:

- **Carrying-capacity assessment** at the twelve highest-pressure sites — ecological, physical, infrastructural and social thresholds, each expressed as a number with a stated confidence interval;
- **Leakage and value-chain study** — where each unit of visitor spend goes, by category, ownership and residence of owner;
- **Resident sentiment baseline** in fourteen localities, disaggregated by age, gender and livelihood, before any promotion begins, so that later movement is interpretable;
- **Consent and tenure mapping** — who holds what rights over which sites, formally and customarily, and where those two registers disagree;
- **Heritage condition survey** — structural and fabric baseline, with footfall sensitivity noted;
- **Water and waste stress test** against three projected peak-load scenarios.

Cost **$620K**. If the study finds that leakage exceeds 55% or that any of the four flagship sites is within 15% of an ecological threshold, the Year 2 promotion envelope should be redirected to supply-side development and capacity works, and the pilot scope revised before commitment. This is the cheapest consequential decision in the programme.

### 2.3 The uncomfortable question, answered rather than deferred

Will the agency be bound by the same entitlements it asks of others? If a district discovers that the agency can overturn a locally-taken decision without giving reasons — or can license a resort inside a locality that declined one — the framework becomes rhetoric and everything downstream of it is wasted. §9.3 answers this with a specific, testable, reportable mechanism, and we would ask the board to adopt or amend it rather than to note it.

---

## 3. What is fixed everywhere: four entitlements, stated as floors

Framed as what a place and its residents are entitled to, rather than as how an operator must behave, so that very different arrangements can honour them.

### 3.1 Entitlement I — ecological ceilings are numbers, and they bind
**Floor:** every designated site has a published maximum daily and peak-hour visitor number, derived from measured thresholds, reviewed annually, and enforceable against every operator including state-owned ones. Where measurement is incomplete, an interim ceiling is set at the conservative end and revised upward only on evidence — never downward under commercial pressure alone.

*The ceiling is the ceiling. A ceiling that rises whenever it is reached is not a ceiling; it is a queue-management aspiration.*

### 3.2 Entitlement II — local value capture has a floor, not an aspiration
**Floor:** in any licensed tourism operation above a defined size, (a) a minimum share of employment at supervisory level and above is held by residents of the district, on a stated glide path rather than immediately; (b) a minimum share of food, craft and service procurement is sourced within the region, verified by audit rather than by declaration; (c) concession revenue from public land and heritage sites returns a defined percentage to the locality under local control.

We would suggest glide paths with dated milestones rather than day-one quotas. A quota that cannot be met produces either non-compliance or imported "residents"; a glide path with a funded training pipeline produces the outcome the quota was reaching for.

### 3.3 Entitlement III — cultural authorship, including the right to withhold
**Floor:** the community associated with a cultural practice, site or artefact decides what is presented to visitors, in what form, at what price, and whether it is presented at all. This includes an unconditional **right to withhold** — some things are not products, and a framework that cannot say so will eventually be asked to sell them.

Practically: no ceremony scheduled for visitor convenience without the custodians' initiative; no photography where custodians have declined it; interpretation texts approved by the community before publication, in their language first; sacred and restricted sites may be closed permanently and that closure is not appealable on commercial grounds.

### 3.4 Entitlement IV — there is a route for grievance, and it is answered
**Floor:** every resident of a tourism locality has at least one accessible channel through which they can object to a tourism development, operator behaviour or agency decision **and receive a dated, substantive response**. Form is local: a village assembly, a district ombudsman, a written pre-read, a monthly market-day surgery, an SMS line. The *answered* part is the floor; the form is entirely local.

**Firewall, mandatory:** this channel is expressly **not** a corruption or safeguarding reporting channel. Objection to a development is not a protected disclosure. The two must be separately named, separately routed and separately governed, or we create legal exposure on one side and chill genuine reporting on the other (§12.4).

### 3.5 Everything else is local property
Product design, pricing, interpretation, ceremony, sequencing, symbolism, tooling, partner selection, target segments, pace, and the destination's own name.

### 3.6 The alternative-form process (in place of exemption)

We deliberately avoid the word *exemption*, and avoid asking any district to refuse. A locality that cannot meet a floor is asked instead to **propose the nearest form it can honour**, and to state what it would take to close the remainder.

| Element | Provision |
|---|---|
| Trigger | Legal impossibility, tenure conflict, or structural impossibility (not difficulty, not commercial inconvenience) |
| Form | Two pages: which floor, why, the alternative mechanism proposed, and the condition under which the floor becomes reachable |
| Approver | Chief Executive of the agency, countersigned by the district authority and the relevant sectoral regulator |
| Duration | **24 months maximum**, renewable once with fresh reasoning |
| Visibility | Entered in a publicly accessible register, reviewed quarterly by the Stewardship Council |
| Presumption | An alternative form is accepted unless materially weaker than the floor. We expect three to six across the network in Year 1 and would be suspicious of zero |
| Never available | Entitlement I ecological ceilings, and the right to withhold under III. These two do not admit alternative forms |

---

## 4. The adaptation logic

### 4.1 Four variables, rather than a general destination model

We would ask each locality to place itself on four axes only, because these four determine whether a given tourism form functions or backfires.

| Axis | The question | What it changes |
|---|---|---|
| **Fragility** | How quickly does damage become irreversible? | Whether the instrument is a cap and permit, or a price signal |
| **Livedness** | Is the site inhabited, worked and used, or is it a monument? | Whether residents can be zoned around, or must be the authors |
| **Existing load** | Is the locality below capacity, near it, or past it? | Whether the task is attraction or de-load — opposite disciplines |
| **Local enterprise depth** | Can local businesses supply what visitors need today? | Whether promotion creates income or creates imports |

### 4.2 The working rule

> Fragility and high existing load do not mean tourism is unwelcome. They mean the growth has to be **in value rather than in volume** — fewer visitors, longer stays, higher spend, deeper local sourcing, dispersed across geography and season.

The functioning equivalent of a marketing campaign, in a locality already at load, is a permit system with dynamic pricing, a second and third route that draws pressure outward, and a shoulder-season product that gives residents twelve months of work instead of four. Our practitioner judgement is that a single well-designed dispersal route moves more economic benefit than a quarter of promotional spend — offered as judgement, not as measured finding (§16), and testable inside the pilots.

### 4.3 Local leadership: a default with a visible opt-out

**Default:** locality-level programme leadership sits with people already running functioning local enterprises or already holding custodial responsibility — selected on observed practice rather than on office held.

A district wishing to depart from this default does so through a one-page note countersigned by the district authority and the programme director, logged in the same register as §3.6. Departures are expected and unremarkable; what matters is that they are visible.

Where the practitioner lead sits outside formal authority, the workable form is almost always a **pair** — the office-holder as visible patron providing cover, the practitioner as the working engine. A practitioner without a patron will in several districts be read, reasonably, as the agency not taking the district seriously.

---

## 5. Using the locality cards well

### 5.1 What they are
Starting hypotheses about context, to be returned marked up within 60 days. They describe patterns we have observed in destinations, not judgements about people.

### 5.2 What each card contains
Working hypothesis on the four axes · where the binding constraint likely sits · what to build · what to decline · failure mode · **leading indicator observable by day 90** · legal, tenure or consent watch item.

### 5.3 The supersession rule
**Where locality-level diagnostic data exists, it supersedes the card, and the card is retired for that locality.** Within-district variance routinely exceeds between-district variance; a single village's history with an earlier development frequently dominates every regional generalisation we could offer.

---

## 6. Locality typology cards

### Card A — Fragile ecosystem, low current load
| | |
|---|---|
| Hypothesis | High fragility; uninhabited or lightly inhabited; well below load; thin local enterprise base |
| Binding constraint | Absence of a ceiling *before* discovery. Once a site is popular, imposing a cap is a political act; before, it is administration |
| Build | Permit system with dynamic pricing and advance ballot; mandatory accredited local guiding; hardened trails and viewing infrastructure ahead of demand; a research and monitoring station co-located with the visitor function |
| Decline | Road upgrades that reduce journey time below the friction the ecosystem depends on; any accommodation inside the boundary; cruise or coach access without a berth/slot cap |
| Failure mode | Single viral image, arrivals treble in eighteen months, ceiling set retrospectively

**2.1 A self-created conflict of interest the document does not notice.** The levy allocates **10% to administration** — i.e. the agency's own budget scales with visitor volume — while the same agency chairs the body that reviews ecological ceilings and holds §3.6 approval authority. §3.1 permits ceilings to be "revised upward only on evidence," but names no independent evidence assessor. **2.2 The agency likely lacks the powers it assumes.** Entitlement I claims ceilings "enforceable against every operator including state-owned ones"; Entitlement II sets employment and procurement mandates; §7.2 hypothecates a levy by statute. The document lists those bodies as *consultees* (§12) rather than as co-holders of the instruments. **The Ministry of Finance is not mentioned at all.** Required: a legal instruments annex mapping each entitlement to the statute, regulation, licence condition or intergovernmental agreement that would carry it, with a legislative timeline. **2.3 "Plumbing before posters" has no plumbing budget.** The sequencing rule vetoes promotion until water, waste, sanitation and access are verified against peak load. The total ask is $6.8M + $14.5M. Utility and access capital works across twelve high-pressure sites will exceed that by an order of magnitude in almost any real region. Either the programme funds the works (budget is wrong by 10×) or it does not (in which case the rule is a veto the programme cannot lift, and the whole plan stalls at Year 2). **2.4 The headline target contradicts the diagnostic discipline.** §1 sets retention 35% → 55% off an **assumed** baseline; §2.2 says no design freeze until the leakage study reports. Publishing a target before measuring the baseline is precisely the error the document criticises elsewhere. Present it as an illustrative ambition to be re-set at diagnostic close.

**2.5 The failure test may be unfalsifiable.** "Retention flat (±3pp)" implies value-chain measurement precise to three percentage points. Leakage studies rarely achieve that; sampling error alone will exceed it. State the measurement method, sample and confidence interval, or widen the band. **2.7 "The community" is treated as a settled entity.** Entitlement III grants decisive authority to "the community associated with a practice." A common measurement spine across inverted objectives needs an explicit account of which indicators are directional and which are shared, or the comparison will be meaningless.

The document devolves "which visitors they seek" and "target segments" to districts and communities. Existing hotels, operators, transport cartels and land interests will resist the levy and the procurement floor. There is no coalition strategy, no treatment of existing licences (grandfathering, renewal conditions, transition period), and no compensation or adjustment logic. ## How we would ask you to use this

One note, then the substance.

This document does not propose a marketing campaign. It proposes the conditions under which a marketing campaign would be safe to run, and a sequence in which the campaign comes fourth rather than first. That ordering is the single most consequential thing in these pages (§14.1), and if the Board changes nothing else, we would ask it to weigh that.

The locality material in §6 is offered as **working hypotheses, so that they may be corrected**. Where a district or community has its own data — or simply its own view of what it wants and does not want — that view supersedes ours and the card is retired for that locality (§5.3).

**On cards returned unamended.** An earlier draft of this paragraph said that an unamended card would be read as evidence that no conversation had taken place. Colleagues who read that draft were right to find the tone wrong: it reserved to the centre the right to disbelieve a district's reply, and a programme about local authorship cannot begin by doing that. The revised position is simpler and, we hope, more respectful. **An unamended card is accepted at face value.** What we owe in return is a better invitation: the Secretariat will offer each locality a facilitated session, at a time and in a form of the locality's choosing, and will publish which localities took it up and which did not — without inference either way. If a card returns unamended and the locality declines a session, we proceed on the card and we say plainly, in the record, that the hypothesis is untested. The burden of the conversation is ours, not the district's.

Two courtesies before this travels further. First, that community and traditional-authority representatives see §§3, 9 and 15 and have time to respond in whatever form suits them before the ministerial pack is assembled — a programme about local authorship that arrives in a village fully formed has already contradicted itself, and people will notice that before they notice anything else. Second, that §12 (legal and consent gates) and **Annex A** be walked through with the Ministry of Finance, the environment agency, the antiquities authority, the lands ministry and, where relevant, the national UNESCO commission before any part of this is described publicly. The likeliest single cause of avoidable damage is a well-intentioned announcement that reaches an investor before it reaches the people who live at the site.

**A note on structure.** A reviewer observed that an earlier draft arranged nearly everything in fours — four entitlements, four axes, four pilots, four cards — and that the symmetry was doing rhetorical rather than analytical work. The observation was fair and we have let the structure follow the problem instead: there are now **five entitlements**, **five placement axes**, **four pilots** (four because that is what the Year 1 facilitation budget and the Secretariat's own capacity will honestly carry, and we say so in §11.1), and **six locality typologies**. ### 1.1 The core proposition, and how confident we are in it

Destinations rarely fail from too few visitors. They fail from visitors arriving faster than the capacity to absorb them and faster than the arrangements to retain their money.

*(This is our considered assertion from practitioner experience and from comparative destination histories, not a finding derived from this region's own data — see the evidence key at §16. We flag it because the Board is entitled to know which of our statements are evidenced and which are judgement, and because a Board that cannot tell the difference cannot govern us properly.)*

The specific failure we are trying to avoid is well documented elsewhere and inexpensive to reproduce: a successful campaign; a three-year arrival surge concentrated on four photogenic sites; a housing market that prices out the people whose culture is the attraction; a leakage rate above 60%; and a resident population that has learned to resent the industry before the industry has learned to pay them. That outcome is worse than slow growth, because it consumes the local consent a second attempt would require. Consent, once spent, is not repurchasable at any budget.

## 2. Diagnosis before design

### 2.1 The framing we would gently ask the Board to test

The programme is currently described as *attracting more international visitors*. The available evidence may instead describe a **value-retention and absorptive-capacity** problem wearing a marketing problem's clothing. Only one of those responds to promotion, and we would rather establish which we have before committing eight figures to the wrong one.

| Candidate constraint | What international demand-generation does to it |
|---|---|
| Genuine awareness or distribution deficit in target markets | Resolves it — this is the case where marketing and §8 are the right tools |
| Weak or absent local supply chain (food, guides, crafts, lodging) | **Amplifies harm** — demand met by imports and outside operators; leakage rises |
| Water, waste or sanitation at or near limit | **Amplifies harm** — irreversible ecological cost, and the first visible one |
| Access bottleneck (single road, single airport slot pattern) | Nothing — concentrates load rather than distributing it |
| Concentration on four sites while thirty are unvisited | Worsens — virality compounds concentration |
| Community consent not established, or custodianship contested | Worsens sharply — arrivals become an imposition, and resistance follows |
| Heritage fabric structurally fragile | **Amplifies harm** — footfall damage is cumulative and unfunded |
| Extreme seasonality producing precarious employment | Nothing — needs shoulder-season product design, not shoulder-season adverts |
| Housing stock convertible to short-term let without registration | **Amplifies harm rapidly** — displacement outruns every mitigation built later |

### 2.2 The diagnostic we propose

Twelve weeks. No design freeze and no campaign commitment until it reports.

- **Carrying-capacity assessment** at the twelve highest-pressure sites — ecological, physical, infrastructural and social thresholds, each expressed as a number with a stated confidence interval, produced by the environment agency and an independent scientific panel, **not by us** (§9.5);
- **Leakage and value-chain study** — where each unit of visitor spend goes, by category, ownership and residence of owner; designed to be repeatable annually and reconcilable to a Tourism Satellite Account (§10.6);
- **Resident sentiment baseline** in fourteen localities, disaggregated by age, gender, livelihood and tenure status, before any promotion begins, so later movement is interpretable;
- **Consent and tenure mapping** — who holds which rights over which sites, formally and customarily, and where the two registers disagree. Disagreement is the expected finding, not the exception, and §3.7 exists because of it;
- **Heritage condition survey** — structural and fabric baseline with footfall sensitivity and **climate exposure** noted (§13.5);
- **Water and waste stress test** against three projected peak-load scenarios, with capital cost attached to each remedy so that §7.4 can be costed rather than asserted;
- **Housing and short-term-let baseline** — conversion rate, rent trajectory, transaction ownership, in the four honeypot localities.

Cost **$620K**. Rules already agreed with the Secretariat's own staff: if leakage exceeds 55%, or if any flagship site is within 15% of an ecological threshold, or if short-term-let conversion exceeds 8% of stock in any honeypot, then the Year 2 promotion envelope is redirected to supply-side development, capacity works and housing instruments, and the pilot scope is revised before commitment.
